svg.aria-label: Diagram: how the AWS DevOps Agent integration attaches to AWS Resilience Hub, what standing its output has, and where it sits on the critical path. AWS states that the next generation of Resilience Hub now integrates with AWS DevOps agent, allowing a customer to review failure mode assessment findings, implement mitigations to resolve findings, and review resilience test results. There are two surfaces with opposite shapes. On a failure mode assessment finding the integration is pull-based: a Chat with DevOps Agent option is available on every failure mode assessment finding, the console opens an interactive session seeded with that finding, the finding's context is already in place, and nothing happens unless the customer asks. On a resilience test the integration is push-based and automatic: when a test is run, Resilience Hub launches a DevOps Agent investigation that observes the test and returns a structured analysis, the investigation starts automatically with the test run, and a summary of its analysis becomes available shortly after the test completes. The analysis can uncover symptoms, root cause and impact along with observed recovery actions such as an ARC Region switch, and the console shows the investigation's verdict, confidence and analysis summary. The central point of the post concerns the standing of that output. AWS states that the DevOps Agent verdict is advisory and that the test run's own result remains authoritative, which is the correct separation, because an agent that could overturn a deterministic test result would make the test unusable as evidence. At the same time AWS states that when a test report is generated for a connected service it includes a DevOps Agent investigation section with the summary, and that test report generation completes when DevOps Agent completes the investigation. So the advisory component is a dependency of the authoritative artefact: the component that cannot change the answer can still delay the document, which matters for anyone whose compliance or change process consumes the test report on a schedule. On identity the integration is deliberately minimal and the documentation is specific. Resilience Hub connects to the Agent Space by assuming the customer's existing invoker role, the same cross-account role that resource discovery already uses, and the customer does not create a new role or change its trust policy. Only permissions are added: eight actions across two statements, five in an investigation statement covering CreateBacklogTask, GetBacklogTask, ListExecutions, ListJournalRecords and UpdateBacklogTask, and three in a validation statement covering GetAgentSpace, GetOperatorApp and ListAssociations. AWS states that these eight actions are the complete set that Resilience Hub calls on the customer's behalf and that none of them can mutate the Agent Space or the customer's resources, and warns against attaching the broad managed policies AIDevOpsAgentFullAccess or AIDevOpsOperatorAppAccessPolicy because they grant mutating Agent Space actions that Resilience Hub must never call. The documented failure mode is that if the invoker role is missing these permissions the connection fails with an access denied error and the service's DevOps Agent status becomes FAILED with a reason telling the customer to update the role, which AWS identifies as the most common cause of a failed connection. Connection is per service, by providing the Agent Space ARN in the service's DevOps Agent configuration, and disconnection is by updating it with an empty configuration, which clears the connection without affecting the Agent Space. Resilience Hub is available in fifteen AWS Regions and DevOps Agent can investigate resources in any Region regardless of where the Agent Space is created. The recommended actions are to add only the eight named actions rather than the broad managed policies, to connect one non-critical service first and read a few investigations against tests whose outcome is already understood, to check whether any schedule depends on test report timing before connecting, and to keep the advisory-versus-authoritative distinction in the runbook where the person reading the console will see it.
svg.title: The verdict cannot change the result, and the report still waits for it
svg.text: An investigation that decides nothing, between you and the document that does.
AWS DevOps Agent in the next generation of Resilience Hub — automatic on every test run, once a service is connected.
ON A FINDING — pull. You ask.
“Chat with DevOps Agent”, “available on every
failure mode assessment finding”.
Session opens with “the finding's context
already in place”. Nothing runs unasked.
ON A TEST RUN — push. It just happens.
An investigation “starts automatically with
the test run” — no per-run flag.
It “observes the test and returns a structured
analysis”: symptoms, root cause, impact.
Two sentences, one page apart. The separation is right. The dependency runs the other way.
“The DevOps Agent verdict is advisory; your test run's own result remains authoritative.”
“The test report generation completes when DevOps Agent completes the investigation.”
The component that cannot change the answer can still hold up the document. Worth knowing if a schedule
collects that report — a DR evidence pack, a change attachment, a compliance upload.
The identity design is the part to copy. No new role, no trust policy change, eight named actions.
“assuming your existing invoker role — the same cross-account role that resource discovery uses”
Investigation (5) CreateBacklogTask GetBacklogTask ListExecutions ListJournalRecords UpdateBacklogTask
Validation (3) GetAgentSpace GetOperatorApp ListAssociations
“None of them can mutate your Agent Space, or your resources.”
And rarer still: “Do not attach the broad AWS managed policies” — AWS names them so you do not reach for them.
What change review will not see
The discovery role already reaches your estate.
It just got wider. The trust policy did not
change, so nothing flags it. Record it yourself.
The named failure, and the clean exit
Missing permissions → status FAILED, “the most
common cause of a failed connection”.
Disconnect per service with an empty config.
Pilot one service. Read the first few investigations against a test whose outcome you can already explain.
That is calibration, not evaluation — and a plausible answer is much harder to disbelieve than a blank page.
